Something happens to a meeting between the room and the record, and almost nobody notices it happening. In the room there were eight people, four subjects and a lot of half sentences. On the page there are five lines and every one of them is finished. That is not dishonesty; it is what writing does. The trouble is that from Monday morning the five lines are the meeting, for everybody who was not there and, within about a fortnight, for most of the people who were. So the interesting question is not whether the record is accurate. It is who chose which four things out of forty were worth a line, and whether the person who disagreed got a sentence or got left out. If you have never volunteered to write the minutes of a meeting you care about, you have been giving that job away for free.

I once got a client into a small argument by choosing one verb. He had said, in a call, that he would try to get the figures over before the end of the week. I passed that on to my own team as he promised the figures by Friday. Same information, roughly, and a completely different sentence. My team planned around Friday. Friday came and went. And when I went back to him he was, quite correctly, confused, because he had never promised anything. He had said he would try. What I learned is that in reported speech the verb you pick is not decoration around the message. It IS the message. He said, he suggested, he admitted, he promised, he agreed. Five verbs, one event, five different weeks for everybody who reads it.
